name: Ghost Dance
info: The Ghost Dance is a ceremony taught from 1889 by the Northern Paiute prophet Wovoka, who held that it would reunite the living with the dead and end Westward expansion; it spread across the Western United States.

facts.where: begun among the Northern Paiute of Mason Valley, Nevada; spread across much of the western United States, reaching California and Oklahoma; the Lakota reservations of South Dakota were the setting of Sitting Bull's death and the Wounded Knee Massacre
facts.period: Wodziwob's dances of 1869; Wovoka's vision of 1 January 1889; spread and the Lakota ghost shirts in 1890; Wounded Knee on 29 December 1890; afterwards clandestine; still practised, most notably by the Caddo
facts.figures: Wovoka (Jack Wilson), the Northern Paiute prophet; Hawthorne Wodziwob, who preached a similar vision in 1869; Tavibo, a weather doctor and Wovoka's father; Kicking Bear, who is believed to have introduced ghost shirts to the Lakota; Short Bull, a spiritual leader; Sitting Bull, the Hunkpapa spiritual leader whom Agent McLaughlin called the real leader; James Mooney, the anthropologist who interviewed Wovoka
facts.outcome: the movement was feared by reservation agents and followed by the arrest and death of Sitting Bull and the Wounded Knee Massacre, in which 200-300 Lakota were killed; open practice declined and the ceremony went underground rather than ending

t: According to Wovoka's teaching, as the anthropologist James Mooney recorded it, a five-day dance performed at the proper intervals would hasten the reunion of the living and the dead and bring a world without sickness, disease or old age.

The Lakota took up the dance in 1890 as the government cut their land and halved their rations; their version was directed towards millenarianism, an innovation that distinguished it from Wovoka's original teachings.
After Sitting Bull's death on 15 December 1890 and the Wounded Knee Massacre on 29 December, open practice declined, but the ceremony became clandestine and the Caddo still practise it today.
dyk: A small set of Ghost Dance songs, curated by James Mooney, was recorded and pressed in 1894, soon after the commercialisation of Emile Berliner's Gramophone; the original masters are held at the Library of Congress.
ev: Hawthorne Wodziwob organises dances among the Paiute to announce a vision of the land of the dead
Wovoka has a vision during a solar eclipse on 1 January, and the Ghost Dance is first practised by the Nevada Northern Paiute
The government breaks up the Great Sioux Reservation into five smaller reservations, and the Lakota rations are cut in half
Sitting Bull is arrested and shot on 15 December, in an exchange in which men on both sides are killed
The Wounded Knee Massacre on 29 December leaves 200-300 Lakota dead, most of them women and children, and 25 US soldiers
A set of Ghost Dance songs curated by James Mooney is recorded and pressed
Lakota men and women, among them Mary Brave Bird, dance the Ghost Dance at Wounded Knee during the occupation
Congress officially apologises for the Wounded Knee Massacre without rescinding any Medal of Honor

sections.background:
The Northern Paiutes of Mason Valley, in what became the state of Nevada, were known collectively as the Tövusidökadö (literally 'grass bulb eaters') at the time of European contact. They lived by fishing, hunting wild game and foraging for pine nuts and roots, and followed various spiritual leaders and community organisers. Community events centred on seasonal ceremonies such as harvests or hunting.

A typhoid fever epidemic struck in 1867. This and other diseases more common among the European population killed approximately one-tenth of the total population and caused widespread psychological and emotional trauma. The disruption brought disorder to the economic system and to society, and many families were prevented from continuing their nomadic lifestyle.

In 1869 Hawthorne Wodziwob, a Paiute man, organised a series of community dances to announce a vision. He spoke of a journey to the land of the dead and of promises made to him by the souls of the recently deceased, who said they would return to their loved ones within three to four years. His peers accepted the vision, likely because of his standing as a healer. He urged the people to dance the common circle dance and preached for three years, helped by a local 'weather doctor' named Tavibo, the father of Wovoka.
sections.aims:
Wovoka, a Northern Paiute spiritual leader also known as Jack Wilson, was believed to have had a vision during a solar eclipse on 1 January 1889. He preached a message of universal love and often presided over circle dances, which symbolised the sun's path across the sky. According to the millenarian teachings attributed to him, proper practice of the dance would reunite the living with the spirits of the dead, bring the spirits to fight on their behalf, end American Westward expansion, and bring peace, prosperity and unity to Native American peoples.

James Mooney, who interviewed Wovoka, reported that Wilson's letter said he had stood before God in heaven and seen many of his ancestors, and that God had told him to return and tell his people to love each other and not fight. They must work, not steal or lie, and give up war and the traditional self-mutilation connected with mourning. If they kept these rules they would be united with their friends and family in the other world, where there would be no sickness, disease or old age. Mooney wrote that the dance was given to Wilson to take to his people, and that if the five-day dance was performed at the proper intervals it would hasten the reunion of the living and the dead.

Wovoka claimed to have left God's presence convinced that if every Indian in the West danced the new dance, all evil would be swept away, leaving a renewed Earth of food, love and faith. The Paiute called it 'Dance In A Circle'; the Lakota expression 'Spirit Dance' was adopted for all such practices and translated as 'Ghost Dance'.
sections.events:
The Ghost Dance was first practised by the Nevada Northern Paiute in 1889. Through Native Americans and some white settlers the message spread across much of the western United States, reaching areas of California and Oklahoma. Many tribes sent members to investigate the prophet, and many left as believers and returned home preaching his message. Mormons from Utah also investigated it, for whom the concepts of the Indian prophet were familiar and often accepted. Different tribes combined selected aspects of the ritual with their own beliefs.

Among the Lakota, ghost shirts were developed: special clothing that warriors could wear, rumoured to repel bullets through spiritual power. It is uncertain where the belief began. Scholars believe that Kicking Bear introduced it to the Lakota in 1890; Mooney argued that the most likely source was the Latter-day Saint temple garment.

In February 1890 the United States government broke a Lakota treaty by splitting the Great Sioux Reservation into five smaller ones, to make room for white homesteaders. The farming plan failed in the semi-arid land, and after the hot, dry growing season of 1890 the government cut Lakota rations in half, at a time when the bison had been virtually eradicated. The people turned to the Ghost Dance, which frightened the agents of the Bureau of Indian Affairs. Kicking Bear was forced to leave Standing Rock, and Agent James McLaughlin asked for more troops. Thousands of additional soldiers were sent to the reservation.
sections.people:
Wovoka, whom Mooney called by his English name Jack Wilson, was the prophet of the movement. He had been trained by an experienced holy man at his parents' direction, after they saw that he had difficulty interpreting his earlier visions, and was also training as a weather doctor like his father Tavibo. He was known throughout Mason Valley as a gifted and blessed young leader. He told Mooney that the Creator had given him power over the weather and made him the deputy in charge of affairs in the western United States. After 1890 Wovoka continued to spread the message, along with Kicking Bear, Short Bull and other spiritual leaders.

Hawthorne Wodziwob and Tavibo had preached a similar vision in 1869. Among the Lakota, Kicking Bear is believed to have introduced the ghost shirt. Agent McLaughlin claimed that the Hunkpapa spiritual leader Sitting Bull was the real leader of the movement. A former agent, Valentine McGillycuddy, saw nothing extraordinary in the dances and ridiculed the panic, comparing the dancers to Seventh-day Adventists preparing ascension robes, whom the army did not move to stop.

Spotted Elk (Big Foot), a Miniconjou leader, was on the army's list of 'trouble-making' Indians. James Mooney, the anthropologist, studied the movement and compared letters passed between tribes. Eyewitness accounts from before Wounded Knee include those of Ella Cara Deloria and Elaine and Dora Goodale.
sections.outcomes:
On 15 December 1890 Sitting Bull was arrested for failing to stop his people from practising the Ghost Dance. One of his men, Catch the Bear, fired at Lieutenant 'Bull Head', who then shot Sitting Bull; the exchange caused deaths on both sides, including Sitting Bull's.

Spotted Elk was stopped while on his way to meet the remaining Lakota chiefs, and the army moved his band to a camp near the Pine Ridge Agency, where the band put up its tipis on the banks of Wounded Knee Creek on the evening of 28 December. The next day officers tried to collect the band's weapons. A young deaf Lakota man refused to give up his, a struggle followed, and a weapon went off into the air. An officer ordered his men to open fire, and the Lakota took up weapons that had been confiscated. US forces fired carbines and Hotchkiss guns mounted on the hill above. When the fighting ended, 200-300 Lakota had been massacred by US soldiers, most of them women and children. Twenty-five soldiers died, many killed by friendly fire. Kicking Bear then surrendered his weapon to General Nelson A. Miles.

Twenty soldiers received the Medal of Honor (some sources say 18 or 23). Activists called these 'Medals of Dis-Honor' and asked for them to be rescinded, but none has been. Open participation in the Ghost Dance declined gradually for fear of more violence, and the ceremony became clandestine. The Navajo did not take it up: their leaders called it 'worthless words' in 1890, and Alice Beck Kehoe attributed this to their relative social and economic satisfaction and to their fear of ghosts and spirits.
sections.legacy:
The Wounded Knee Massacre was not the end of the Ghost Dance. It went underground, and it is practised today most notably by the Caddo, though details are confined to the participants. Practice of the movement was believed to have contributed to Lakota resistance to assimilation under the Dawes Act. In 1973, during the Wounded Knee occupation, Lakota men and women, including Mary Brave Bird, danced the Ghost Dance on the site where their ancestors had been killed; Brave Bird wrote in Lakota Woman that ghost dances continue as private ceremonies. Congress officially apologised for the massacre in 1990 but did not rescind any Medal of Honor.

The dance was also taken up by the entertainment of the time. A small set of Ghost Dance songs was recorded and pressed in 1894 under Mooney's direction, and it is unclear who sang them, possibly Mooney himself. Edison's Kinetoscope showed a 22-second film called Sioux Ghost Dance, which gave non-Native viewers an inaccurate picture: it included a drum, though the dance itself uses no instruments, and the dancers moved fast with their heads down, where the original dance is slow, with hands held together and heads usually looking upward.

Native performers in Buffalo Bill's Wild West shows were generally paid the same as other performers and encouraged to keep their language and rituals, yet were stereotyped as mounted, war-bonneted warriors and had to refight a losing war nightly.

summary: The Ghost Dance was a ceremony taught from 1889 by the Northern Paiute prophet Wovoka, who held that it would reunite the living with the dead and end Westward expansion. The Lakota took it up in 1890; Sitting Bull's death and the Wounded Knee Massacre followed, and the ceremony became clandestine but is still practised.
references: Alice Beck Kehoe, The Ghost Dance: Ethnohistory and Revitalization (Waveland Press, 2006)
notes: Dates: the article gives 1889 as the first practice among the Nevada Northern Paiute; Wodziwob's dances of 1869 are told as background. Start 1889; end null because the Caddo still practise it.

The article contradicts itself on Spotted Elk: he was 'stopped' on December 29, but the band camped 'that evening, December 28', and the massacre was 'the following day'. I left out the date of the stopping, said the band camped on the evening of 28 December, and dated the massacre 29 December ('the following day'), which the article implies but does not state outright.
The Wounded Knee death toll: article says 200-300 Lakota massacred, most women and children; 25 US soldiers dead, many by friendly fire. Medal of Honor count: 20, with 18 or 23 in some sources.

The article says the Lakota interpretation removed all European Americans from their lands and quotes a passage (p. 228, source unnamed) about the earth rolling up like a carpet; I left it out because the quoted author is not named.

Left out: the Round Dance and Leslie Spier's 'prophet dances' section, the detailed description of the ceremony itself (sweat lodges, eagle-wing fans, trance) and the Leonard Crow Dog chant, for length; the See also list (Boxer Rebellion, Mumboism and others) is not taken as part of this movement.
Wovoka's name for the Lakota-derived title: article says 'Spirit Dance' was the Lakota expression and was translated as 'Ghost Dance'.
References left empty as instructed; the article's Further reading lists Andersson 2009, Brown 2001, Du Bois 2007, Gage 2020, Kehoe 2006, Osterreich 1991, Stannard 1993 and Warren 2017.
